# Problem 3, firework bursts: three options

## MEASURED A/B (2026-09-01, runtime-patched live page, SwiftShader; gains in ms per frame vs same-load baseline; 4x = CPU-throttled weak-machine proxy; control drift 0.4ms at 1x, 0.04ms at 4x)

Burst protocol: 8 shells spawned, sampled during the explosions, at the top of About, 4x throttle (the spiking environment).
- **Option A shells-out-of-reflection: burst p95 33.3 -> 16.8 - the dropped frame during bursts is GONE.** Avg +0.5.
- **Option B trail 10 -> 5: burst p95 33.3 -> 16.8 - also kills the spike on its own.** Avg +0.8.
- Option B trail 10 -> 7: p95 stays 33.3 - seven copies does NOT clear the frame budget; five does. If the trail look survives at 5, pick 5; 7 buys the look but not the frame.
- Either A or B alone is enough on this machine; both together is headroom for weaker ones.

---


Scope: every option below touches only shell rendering cost. The scene's only `FireworkController` lives on the full preset (`_javascript/three-background-scene.js:28`); the minimal preset has no fireworks (`_javascript/three-background-minimal.js:1-4`), so nothing here can move a pixel on post or section pages. The `fireworks-reach.js` runtime patch overrides only `createAutoFirework` and is untouched by all three options (`assets/js/effects/fireworks-reach.js:47`).

## The sanity check first: where the cost actually is

MEASURED + arithmetic from code. `sizeAttenuation: true` (firework-controller.js:293), material size starts at 25 (firework-controller.js:464: `20 * (1 - 0) + 5`), three.js multiplies size by the 0.5 pixel ratio and uses half the logical viewport height (805 / 2) as the attenuation scale (INFERENCE, three.js internals). Shells sit 3500 to 5000 units from the camera (three-config.js:95-96, camera z 500). So a point is `12.5 * 402.5 / 3500..5000` = **0.9 to 1.4 px**, and trail ghosts taper to 0.55 of that (firework-controller.js:389). In the quarter-scale reflection target they are sub-pixel. Each of a shell's 4,000 points touches 1 to 4 pixels, half discarded by the circular mask, so fragment cost is a few thousand pixels per shell, trivial. **Vertex-shader invocations, draw submission, the 80 to 144 KB birth upload, and the program recompile are the entire cost.** That is why the three options below attack vertex count, pass count, and compile count, and none of them touch the fragment shader.

Per-shell arithmetic used throughout: 400 particles x trail 10 = 4,000 vertices, drawn twice (main pass + reflection pass, mirroredSurface.js:328-329) = 8,000 vertex invocations and 2 draw calls per shell per frame. Birth buffers: position 48 KB + delay 32 KB = 80 KB solid, +64 KB colour = 144 KB rainbow (firework-controller.js:237-241). MEASURED: 8 shells push p95 to 33.4 ms against an About-top baseline avg of 17.2, so 8 shells cost roughly 16 ms p95, about 2 ms per shell software-rendered.

---

## Option A: keep shells out of the reflection render (THREE.Layers)

Shells go on layer 1. The main camera opts in, the mirror camera never does (a fresh `PerspectiveCamera` sees only layer 0), so the reflection pass stops drawing every burst a second time.

```diff
--- _javascript/firework-controller.js  (constructor, lines 9-13)
   constructor(scene, camera, config = {}) {
     this.scene = scene;
     this.camera = camera;
+    // Shells live on layer 1. The main camera opts in here; the water reflection
+    // camera sees only layer 0, so a burst is never drawn again into the mirror.
+    camera.layers.enable(1);
     this.fireWorkGroup = [];
```

```diff
--- _javascript/firework-controller.js  (createPoints, line 278)
     const points = new THREE.Points(geometry, material);
+    points.layers.set(1); // reflection skips shells, see the constructor note
     points.userData.time = timeUniform;
```

Optional third hunk, a no-op that states the rule where the mirror renders (mirroredSurface.js:40):

```diff
     this.mirrorCamera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(camera.fov * 1, camera.aspect, 0.001, camera.far);
+    // Layer 0 only (the constructor default). Written out because it is a rule, not an
+    // accident: fireworks are on layer 1 and must never render into the reflection.
+    this.mirrorCamera.layers.set(0);
```

- **Predicted saving** (INFERENCE from the measured 16 ms / 8 shells, both passes vertex-bound so roughly half each): removes 4,000 of each shell's 8,000 vertex invocations plus one reflection draw call per live shell. 8-shell p95 33.4 -> roughly 26 to 28. Also trims 1 draw call per live shell off the bottom-of-scroll 104-118. Birth spike unchanged.
- **Visual risk: subtle.** The water loses the faint firework shimmer. At quarter reflection scale through the distortion the shells were sub-pixel dots, so it is likely already invisible, but **Rod looks once**: bottom of the About scroll during a burst, water in view. Bloom is unaffected (shells still render in the main pass that feeds it). The water-click raycast targets the water mesh on layer 0, unaffected (three-background-scene.js:76).
- **Not recommended sub-option:** also layering the 25 embers out of the reflection (three-background-scene.js:89-110) would save ~25 reflection draw calls but visibly deletes the firefly reflections floating over the water. That one is a taste call, not a perf freebie.
- **Line delta:** +4 in the controller (2 code, 2 comment), optional +3 in mirroredSurface. D5: two code lines, no state, no branches, deletes an entire render of every shell.
- **Prefer when:** you want the biggest steady-state cut with the least visible change.

## Option B: trail copies 10 -> 5 (or 7)

One knob. Trail count multiplies everything: vertices in both passes, birth buffer size, and buffer-build loop iterations (firework-controller.js:55, 237-241, 272).

```diff
--- _javascript/three-config.js  (fireworks block, after line 96)
     minZ: -3000,
     maxZ: -4500,
+
+    // Ghost copies per particle. Multiplies shell vertex count: 400 particles x 5 = 2000
+    // vertices per shell. Was 10 (4000); halved because software renderers pay per vertex.
+    particleTrail: 5,
```

(Zero-line alternative: change the default `10` to `5` at firework-controller.js:55. The config version costs one line but keeps the knob where the other firework tunables live, matching the "single source of truth" header at three-config.js:1-2.)

- **Arithmetic.** N=5: 2,000 verts/shell, 4,000 invocations with the reflection, half of today; birth buffers 40 KB solid / 72 KB rainbow, build loop 4,000 -> 2,000 iterations. N=7: 2,800 verts/shell, minus 30% everywhere, buffers 56 / 101 KB.
- **Predicted saving** (INFERENCE, cost linear in vertex count since fragments are trivial, see sanity check): N=5 takes 8-shell p95 33.4 -> roughly 26, same class as Option A, and unlike A it also shrinks the birth part of the throttled-portal 99.9 ms spikes (build + upload halves; the compile part remains, that is Option C's job). N=7 -> roughly 28 to 29.
- **Visual risk: visible, briefly.** Ghost copies are 0.005 of normalized burst time apart (firework-controller.js:236, 257) and the burst runs 0 -> 1 over 1.2 s (firework-controller.js:457-459), so each copy trails 6 ms of motion. Ten copies smear 54 ms of travel, which at burst opening speed is an 8 to 24 px streak; five copies smear 24 ms, so **the opening frames of each burst lose about half their streak length** (4 to 11 px). Late in the burst the particles have slowed and the ghosts mostly overlap, so drift and fade look the same. The tail taper also ends at 0.8x size instead of 0.55x. **Rod looks once**: click a shell, watch the first half second. N=7 is the hedge if 5 reads too crisp.
- **Line delta:** +1 (or 0). D5: removes work by changing a number.
- **Prefer when:** the reflection shimmer must stay, or you want the birth spike shaved too.

## Option C: pin the shell program + cap maxFireworks at 12

Two independent one-shot fixes for the spikes rather than the steady state.

**C1, program pin.** Every shell builds its own material; when the last live shell dies, `material.dispose()` (firework-controller.js:482) drops the shared GL program's refcount to zero and three.js deletes it, so the next shell recompiles, a whole-frame hitch on software GL (the 99.9 ms class). Fix: keep the first dead shell's material per colour mode forever. An undisposed, once-rendered material holds the program reference, so the cached program survives empty skies (INFERENCE, three.js program refcounting; the two colour modes compile two distinct programs because `vertexColors` differs, firework-controller.js:295).

```diff
--- _javascript/firework-controller.js  (constructor, line 80)
     this._removeGroup = []; // reused each frame (avoid per-frame array allocation)
+    // One dead shell's material per colour mode is kept forever (see the cleanup loop).
+    // It pins the compiled GL program so the first shell after an empty sky reuses it
+    // instead of recompiling, which is a whole-frame hitch on software GL.
+    this._warmMaterials = { solid: null, rainbow: null };
```

```diff
--- _javascript/firework-controller.js  (cleanup loop, lines 479-483)
         if (firework.explosion) {
           this.scene.remove(firework.explosion);
           firework.explosion.geometry.dispose();
-          firework.explosion.material.dispose();
+          const slot = firework.isRainbow ? 'rainbow' : 'solid';
+          if (this._warmMaterials[slot]) firework.explosion.material.dispose();
+          else this._warmMaterials[slot] = firework.explosion.material;
         }
```

`clear()` (firework-controller.js:494-503) needs no change: it only disposes live shells' materials, and a pinned material always belongs to an already-removed shell. The rejected variant (a hidden 1-particle warm `Points` in the scene) was worse under D5: more lines, a permanent scene object, and a draw call.

**C2, cap.** MEASURED: 8 simultaneous shells already cost p95 33.4. The greeting stream caps itself at 4 live (three-config.js:106), so `maxFireworks` only bounds click spam.

```diff
--- _javascript/three-config.js  (line 87)
-    maxFireworks: 50,
+    // 12 not 50: 8 simultaneous software-rendered shells measured 33 ms frames, so this
+    // bounds spam-clicking at 1.5x that load instead of 6x. The greeting caps itself at 4.
+    maxFireworks: 12,
```

- **Predicted saving:** steady frames unchanged. C1 deletes the tallest single frames, the mid-session recompile hitches inside the 99.9 ms throttled-portal class and the first-click hitch after scrolling away from the greeting (birth build/upload spikes remain, Option B's territory). C2 turns the worst possible case from ~6x the measured 8-shell load into ~1.5x. MEASURED context: heap is currently flat; C1 retains exactly two small material objects, bounded, so it stays flat.
- **Visual risk: none** for C1. C2: a spam-clicker hits the ceiling at 12 in-flight shells (a shell lives ~1.5 to 2 s, so that takes ~7 clicks per second); extra clicks silently do nothing, exactly as they do today at 50, just earlier. **Rod looks once**: spam-click and judge whether the ceiling feels stingy.
- **Line delta:** +7 (3 code, 4 comment) plus one value change. D5: this adds a two-slot object and one branch, which the law flags; justified because the hitch it removes is a measured whole-frame stall that no line deletion can remove, and the state is write-once and bounded at two entries.
- **Prefer when:** the complaint is stutter and dropped single frames rather than average frame rate, which is what users actually feel.

---

**Stacking note:** A and B multiply (B halves both passes, A removes the remaining reflection half, shells land at ~25% of today's steady cost); C is orthogonal and fixes what A and B cannot.

**Recommendation:** ship Option A plus Option C (both invisible except one look each at the water shimmer and the spam ceiling), and hold Option B at N=7 in reserve if 8-shell p95 still overshoots after measuring.
